Colombian Agriculture Sector Hit by Major Ransomware Attack, Disrupting Operations Nationwide

A sophisticated ransomware attack has targeted several major agricultural firms across Colombia, halting operations at dozens of processing sites and affecting thousands of workers, according to industry sources. The attack, which began late Sunday evening, has encrypted critical IT systems at multiple companies, leaving farming cooperatives and producers unable to access production data, manage inventories, or process payments.

The National Federation of Agricultural Producers (FENAGRO) confirmed that at least five leading agribusinesses, including AgroCol Sur, CampoFresco, and Granos del Norte, are currently grappling with locked systems. “We are mobilizing every available resource to restore our operations,” said FENAGRO president Luisa Cárdenas in a statement. “This attack has disrupted our processing lines and delayed the dispatch of agricultural products from our facilities. We are working closely with cybersecurity experts and authorities to contain the situation.”

The ransomware, identified by cybersecurity analysts as a variant known for targeting industrial controls, has rendered key management platforms inoperable. As a result, packing and processing plants in Antioquia, Valle del Cauca, and Cundinamarca have suspended shifts, with some sites reporting temporary layoffs. “Our packing facility has been at a standstill since early Monday,” said Juan Esteban Gómez, site manager at CampoFresco’s Rionegro operation. “We are unable to track shipments or coordinate harvesting activities.”

Trade union representatives expressed concern over the impact on the workforce. “More than 4,000 agricultural workers have seen their shifts suspended today,” said Rosa Mendoza, spokesperson for the Agricultural Workers’ Union. “Families are anxious about lost income and job uncertainty. We urge companies to communicate clearly and support affected workers during this crisis.”

Industry analysts warn that the ongoing outage could lead to broader disruptions if systems are not restored swiftly. “Timing is critical, especially as we enter the peak export season for coffee, bananas, and flowers,” commented Andrés Vélez, an independent agriculture consultant. “Any extended downtime risks product spoilage and lost revenues.”

Authorities have launched an investigation but have yet to identify the perpetrators of the attack. The Ministry of Agriculture reiterated its commitment to supporting the sector and called for heightened cybersecurity vigilance. As of Tuesday evening, there was no indication that affected companies had paid any ransom or regained access to their critical data.

FENAGRO advised all agricultural firms to monitor their networks for suspicious activity, urging the industry to “remain alert and prepared for further threats.” Recovery efforts continue as the sector works to restore normal operations.
